readerTitle: Why the store's own label sits right next to the famous brand
caseNote: 실제 관찰 (마트 진열대의 자체 브랜드) + 가상 사례 (식료품점 올리브유, 피자 가게 칠리 오일) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 자체 브랜드는 싼 복제품이 아니라 마진, 공급사와의 협상력, 경쟁사에는 없는 상품이라는 세 가지를 한꺼번에 얻는 운영 도구다.
misconception: 자체 브랜드는 가격에 민감한 손님을 위한 싸구려 상품이라 가게에 남는 돈도 적다.

sources.text: 소매 유통의 표준 개념 (자체 브랜드, private label, 위탁 생산)

factChecks.note: 올리브유 계산: 유명 브랜드 $12 − 매입가 $9 = $3, 자체 브랜드 $9 − 매입가 $5 = $4. 손님은 $3 절약, 가게는 병당 $1 더 남김. 모든 수치는 가상입니다.
'자체 브랜드가 유명 브랜드를 만드는 제조사에서 생산되는 경우가 있다'는 일반적 관찰로만 썼고 특정 기업·제품은 언급하지 않았습니다. 게시 전 표현이 과하지 않은지 확인하세요.
'자체 브랜드의 마진이 유명 브랜드보다 높은 경우가 많다'는 일반론으로 'often'이라고만 적었습니다. 구체적 비율은 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why the store's own label sits right next to the famous brand
body: Walk down any supermarket aisle. Next to the famous pasta sauce sits a jar with the store's own name on it. It's cheaper, and it's placed at eye level.
You'd think the store loses out when you pick the cheaper jar. Often, it's the opposite.

image.label: A famous-brand jar and a store-brand jar side by side on a shelf
image.brief: 마트 진열대 클로즈업. 화려한 라벨의 소스 병과 단순한 라벨의 '가게 이름' 소스 병이 나란히 놓여 있고, 가격표는 각각 $5, $3.50. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A cheaper olive oil with your name on it?
body: You run three grocery stores. Your best-selling olive oil is a famous brand. It sells for $12 and costs you $9.
A regional producer offers to bottle a similar oil under your store's name for $5 a bottle. You could sell it for $9. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it. A cheaper bottle will just pull sales away from the $12 one
options.feedback: You protect the bigger price tag, but you keep only $3 per bottle and stay fully dependent on one supplier.

options.text: Add your own bottle next to the famous brand
options.feedback: Shoppers keep their choice, and you earn more on every bottle that switches. You also gain something to bring to your next talk with the brand.

options.text: Replace the famous brand with your own bottle
options.feedback: You earn more per bottle, but loyal fans of the brand may start buying it, and the rest of their basket, somewhere else.

cards.title: Follow one bottle.
body: The shopper saves $3. The store keeps **$1 more**. Both sides win on the same sale.

cards.title: Store brands
body: A **store brand**, also called a private label, is a product sold under the retailer's own name. Someone else usually makes it under contract.
It isn't just a cheap copy. The store skips much of the brand's advertising cost and middle layers, so it can charge less and still keep more.
Some store brands are even made in the same factories as the famous names they sit beside.

cards.title: One product, three jobs.
body: A good store brand does more than add margin.
list: **More kept per sale:** a lower price, but a lower cost too
**Bargaining power:** a supplier who knows you have an alternative negotiates differently
**Something rivals can't sell:** shoppers can't compare its price elsewhere, and they come back to you for it
cards.callout: The margin is the easy part to see. The other two jobs often matter more.
cards.softwareNote: Online marketplaces do this too: they use their own sales data to launch house-label basics. It works for the same three reasons, but it can cost the trust of the sellers they compete with.

cards.title: The same move, in many shops.
body: Pharmacies sell their own pain relievers. Hardware stores sell their own screws and paint. Clothing stores sell house-label basics.
Restaurants do it with house wine and bottled sauces. A bakery sells jars of its own jam. In each case the business takes a product people already buy from it and puts its own name on the label.

image.label: A pharmacy, hardware store and bakery, each with a house-label product
image.brief: 세 칸 일러스트. 약국의 자체 브랜드 진통제, 철물점의 자체 브랜드 페인트 통, 빵집의 자체 잼 병. 각 상품 라벨에는 'Our own' 같은 일반 문구만. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your name is now on the product.
body: If a branded product fails, customers blame the brand. If your own label fails, they blame you, and that can spill onto everything else you sell.
You also take on new work: picking a maker, testing quality, and meeting minimum orders. A small shop may have to buy far more stock than it can sell quickly.
And launch only where customers already buy a lot. A store brand in a slow category just adds shelf clutter.

cards.title: Now it's a pizzeria.
body: You sell bottles of a well-known chili oil by the register. Customers keep asking for the house chili oil you put on your pizzas.
A local bottler can make it for you, but the lowest price per bottle needs an order of 2,000. What do you do?

options.text: Start with a small batch at a higher unit cost, and keep the known brand on the shelf
options.feedback: You pay a bit more per bottle at first, but you test real demand before your cash and shelf space get tied up.

options.text: Order 2,000 bottles for the best price and drop the known brand
options.feedback: The best unit cost means nothing if bottles sit for a year. You'd also lose the customers who want the brand.

options.text: Keep selling only the known brand. Bottling isn't your business
options.feedback: You avoid new work and risk, but you ignore clear demand for something only you can sell.

cards.title: Your own label earns margin, leverage and loyalty.
body: A store brand works best in a category customers already buy from you often, with quality you're proud to put your name on.
**Try it today:** find your best-selling product made by someone else. Ask what you'd keep per sale if it carried your name.
